entities.summary:
Miguel de Zalba (b. 1374, Pamplona – d. 1406-09-02, Monzón) was a prominent Navarrese cleric and cardinal whose career was inextricably linked to the tumultuous Western Schism, a period of profound ecclesiastical division that saw rival popes vie for legitimacy across Europe. Elevated to the episcopacy at a young age and later to the College of Cardinals by Antipope Benedict XIII, Zalba emerged as a staunch advocate for the Avignon papacy, playing a significant diplomatic and administrative role in an era defined by fractured religious authority and intense political maneuvering among Christian kingdoms. His life reflects the deep entanglement of secular and spiritual power in late medieval Iberia, as well as the challenges faced by figures attempting to navigate a deeply polarized church.

Zalba's early ecclesiastical career saw him become Bishop of Pamplona in 1387, a strategic position in the Kingdom of Navarre, which maintained close ties with the Avignon papacy. His loyalty to Pedro de Luna, who became Benedict XIII in 1394, was unwavering. In 1403, Benedict XIII rewarded Zalba's fidelity by appointing him Cardinal-Deacon of San Giorgio in Velabro. During his cardinalate, Zalba was instrumental in Benedict XIII's efforts to maintain and consolidate support for the Avignon line, particularly within the Iberian Peninsula and parts of France. He participated in various councils and diplomatic missions aimed at resolving the schism, often engaging with secular rulers and other ecclesiastical figures to garner allegiance or mediate disputes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Miguel de Zalba was a significant figure in the Avignon papacy during the Western Schism, contributing to the prolonged division of the Catholic Church through his steadfast loyalty and diplomatic efforts. His career highlights the complex interplay of regional politics and ecclesiastical authority in late medieval Iberia.
